extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (graduate students, postdocs, and early-career researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for mathematicians on how to deeply learn, re-learn, and master a research field so as to produce better research and exposition. Emphasizes iterative mastery via probing, teaching, literature search, and reflective practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep understanding beyond surface knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely knowing a theorem's statement and proof is insufficient; one should 'dig deeper until you really understand what the lemma is all about.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go beyond rote recollection of statements and formal proofs to develop intuition about why results are true and what they really mean. Seek the core ideas and mechanisms rather than only the formal derivation; avoid stopping at superficial familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek alternate proofs and compare them: do different proofs generalize in different ways and what are their relative strengths and weaknesses?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively try to find different proofs or viewpoints for the same result, analyze how each approach behaves under generalization, and catalog trade-offs (clarity, generality, applicability). Using multiple approaches reveals deeper structure and potential extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test foundational assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Question why each hypothesis is necessary and explore generalizations (known, conjectured, or heuristic); determine whether simpler versions suffice for some applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe necessity by seeking counterexamples, weakening hypotheses, or proving converses. Consider both formal generalizations and heuristic/experimental relaxations; this sheds light on the robustness and limits of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify model examples that demonstrate the lemma, determine when it is useful versus unhelpful, and clarify what problems it can or cannot solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map results to concrete examples and applications to understand applicability and limitations. Use examples to test boundaries and to guide where the tool should or should not be applied in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader context
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore analogues in other mathematical areas and identify wider paradigms or programs the concept fits into.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate concepts to similar ideas in other fields, situate results within larger research programs, and look for unifying themes. This cross-field perspective can suggest new lines of inquiry or transfer techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching and writing as a learning tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Lecturing, preparing lecture notes, or writing expository material internalizes difficult results efficiently and frees mental space for advanced learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use preparation for teaching or exposition as an intentional exercise to clarify understanding: explain concepts to others, produce clear notes, and distill arguments. Teaching forces identification of gaps and deepens mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation searching to trace development
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tools (e.g., MathSciNet) to find papers citing key works and discover relevant subsequent research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform backward/forward literature searches to follow how ideas evolved, identify important variants or applications, and discover current directions and open problems tied to a result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective practice: revisit solved problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Return to solved problems rather than moving immediately onward; re-examining past solutions reveals important connections and deeper insights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodically revisit prior work to re-evaluate methods, spot overlooked relationships, and synthesize new perspectives. Reflection converts solved exercises into lasting conceptual knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery is iterative; good exposition reflects re-learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery comes from iterative re-learning; a 'good' exposition is typically written by an author who has re-learned their field, not just learned it once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that clarity and depth in research and exposition usually arise after multiple passes through material. Aim to iteratively refine understanding and presentations rather than expecting one-pass mastery.
